newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - US T-bond vols bounce after note auction.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - US T-bond vols bounce after note auction.

text.p: Implied volatilities for Treasury bond options were a touch firmer in late trade, bouncing mildly from early lows after a sloppy three-year Treasury note auction, traders said.
"We saw some selling (in futures) right after the numbers and vols came back up," said a brokerage trader at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT). "But vols have been really low to start with."
Implied volatility for CBOT June T-bond futures options stood at around 7.6 percent in late trade, up about 0.2 point on the day.
The Treasury announced in the afternoon that its auction of $17 billion in three-year notes produced an average yield of 6.44 percent, with stop at 6.45 percent and bid-to-cover ratio of 2.08 times.
June T-bonds dipped into negative territory after the auction results but managed to continue seesawing narrowly around Monday's 110-1/32 close.

Traders and analysts noted that the body of daily candlesticks, or the open-close spread, was getting smaller and smaller in recent days after the big April 29 rally -- only 1/32 on Monday and perhaps 2/32 or 3/32 today.

While that could be viewed as a sign the market was about to see a near-term pullback, traders said the stagnation was making it difficult for them to hold options, particularly June options, which expire in less than two weeks on May 16.
But with the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on May 20 coming up soon, the market was also wary of being short gamma, they added.
Shorter-dated options have higher time-decay rate but in return have higher gamma, which provides quicker premium acceleration against a change in bond prices.
In Eurodollar options on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), December volatility was slightly firmer after some early bidding, but the rest of the curve was mostly steady.
Implied volatility for December Eurodollar futures options was up 0.2 point at around 11.0 percent.
Traders said there was also good interest in downside strikes in mid-curve options, which are high-gamma options expiring in the near months but priced off 1998 futures.
One firm was said to have traded a short-June 93.25/93.00 put spread in a ratio of 12,000-by-4,000 contracts. Another firm was seen buying 3,000 of 93.25 puts outright.
June 1998 futures stood at 93.43, down two basis points.
An investment bank trader at the CME said traders seemed to be starting to position themselves for the FOMC meeting.
"People are trying to surmise what would be the logical course of action," he said.
